prompt.problem_text: Weighted vertex colouring. Given a graph whose vertices carry positive integer weights, give every vertex a colour so that no edge joins two vertices of the same colour. The COST of a colouring is the sum, over the colours used, of the LARGEST weight among the vertices of that colour; lower is better; the number of colours is free (with all weights equal this is the classical graph colouring problem). An instance file (`<name>.wcol`) has a line `p edge <n> <m>`, one line `n <vertex> <weight>` per vertex (vertices 1..n, numbered by decreasing weight) and one line `e <u> <v>` per edge. A solution file has n lines; line i is the colour (an integer from 0) of vertex i. The evaluation service re-reads the solution file with its own verifier: every vertex coloured, no edge inside a colour, cost recomputed (`python3 tools/problem.py verify <instance> <solution>` in your directory does the same)
prompt.solver_text: a tree search over partial colourings: the vertices are coloured in their file order, one tree level per vertex; every round selects a branch by an upper-confidence rule on the statistics of earlier rounds, expands it by one node, completes the partial colouring (greedily, then by a LOCAL SEARCH that runs for a time proportional to the number of vertices), and feeds the cost back along the branch; branches that cannot beat the best colouring are cut. Open-source C++ in `code/` (`main.cpp` the options; `methods/` the tree search, the greedy completions, several local searches and the helper that picks one when more than one is listed; `representation/` graph, colouring, tree node, parameters; `utils/`), two small header libraries in `ext/` (option parsing, text formatting), and `params.txt` with the options the program is started with (which local search, how the rounds are simulated, the time of one local search = max(1, int(P_time x n) + O_time) whole seconds, the exploration coefficient)
prompt.time_text: 300 seconds of wall-clock time per instance, whatever its size; the program is given `--time_limit 297` and counts whole seconds
prompt.build_text: `code/main.cpp` and every `code/*/*.cpp` compiled with `g++ -O3 -flto=auto -DNDEBUG -std=c++17 -w -Iext -Icode -DFMT_HEADER_ONLY` and linked with `-O3 -flto=auto -s`, after `params.txt` has been checked (lines `option value`; not problem, instance, rand_seed, time_limit, target, output_directory); then the launcher `solver` is written next to the binary; `python3 tools/problem.py build src bin` does exactly this in your directory
prompt.io_text: `solver <instance file> <solution file> -t <seconds> -seed <int>`: the launcher writes the instance as `instances/reduced_wvcp/g.col` (edges) and `g.col.w` (one weight per line) into a working directory, starts the program in its `build/` sub-directory as `prog --problem wvcp --instance g --rand_seed <int> --time_limit <seconds - 3> --target 0 --output_directory <dir> --<each line of params.txt>`, and turns the LAST data line of the program's file `<dir>/g_<seed>.csv` (columns ..., nb_colors, penalty, score, colours joined by `:`) into the solution file; a termination signal lets the program finish its current step and write that line
prompt.size_text: `--n` is the number of vertices (the service asks for sizes from {lo} to {hi}).
